summary: ```markdown # CLO Skills Workshop - The Clever Use of Hierarchical Settings ## Introduction Hello everyone! Today, we will explain the usage of the setting layer tool. The setting layer tool is used to establish the layer relationship between the panels. ## Understanding the Setting Layer Tool ### Concept and Principle The following is an example of a silver panel and a pure panel. First, switch to the texture surface. You can see the front and back of the panel. This side is the front of the panel, while the slightly darker side is the back of the panel. In our first project file, the pure panel is facing outwards, and the silver panel is also facing outwards. Let's use the setting layer tool first. Click on the silver panel and then click on the pure panel. Open the simulation. ### Simulation Results The silver panel is simulated outside the pure panel. At this time, the middle arrow is a plus sign. If we click on it to change it to a minus sign and open the simulation, you can see that the silver panel is simulated inside the pure panel. In summary, if the middle arrow is the plus sign, then the selected panel will be simulated outside the selected panel. Conversely, if it is the minus sign, it indicates the opposite. ## Practical Application in Project Files ### Second Project File Let's open the second project file. In this case, the silver panel is facing outwards, and the pure panel is also facing outwards. We use the setting layer tool to click on the silver panel first and then click on the pure panel. Open the simulation, and you will see that the silver panel is simulated again outside the front of the pure panel. This occurs because the setting layer tool simulates on the panel layer, and the second simulation is influenced by the opposite side of the selected panel. ### Moving vs. Fixed Panels We can see the selected panel as moving, while the other selected panel is fixed. If the middle arrow is the plus sign, then the selected panel will always be simulated outside the front of the selected panel. If it is the minus sign, it indicates the opposite. ## Example: 3D Clothing Simulation Next, let's take this jacket as an example. When we make 3D clothing, the front of the panel is usually facing outwards, and the back of the panel is also facing outwards. When the fabric is made of opposite materials, the effect remains consistent. When the thick texture surface is opened, the display effect of the clothing is not affected. However, this clothing uses a fabric with a clear difference on the opposite side. Its side should face outwards. ### Layer Relationships in Clothing In addition, to simulate a stable wearing effect, we will use the setting layer tool to set the layer relationship between the large panel and the side. We will point the large panel to the side and simulate the outside of the side. In this scenario, if we turn the side over, then the large panel will behave as discussed in the previous demonstration, simulating the outside of the side panel. To achieve the desired display effect, we need to use the setting layer tool, click on the symbol in the arrow, and observe that the plus sign has transformed into a minus sign. Open the simulation again, and you will see that the large panel now simulates the outside of the side panel, which is the display effect we aim to achieve. ## Conclusion Let's look at the simulation results. The time frame is available to calculate like this. These are the MON mountains unveiled this time. It is easy to understand and also simple. For example, when I scroll down, I get the equivalent time frame at the red cell line. ```
